units.title: Earth's Origin and Interior
units.blurb: How Earth formed and sorted into layers, how earthquake waves reveal the inside, and how heat, buoyancy and magnetism shape the crust.

units.title: Minerals
units.blurb: How atoms build crystals, the silicate families that make up most rock, and the other mineral groups.

units.title: Igneous Rocks and Volcanoes
units.blurb: How rock melts, how magma crystallizes and is named, where it cools underground, and why some eruptions explode.

units.title: Sediments and Sedimentary Rocks
units.blurb: How weathering makes sediment, how flowing water sorts it, and how layers record the places they formed.

units.title: Metamorphism
units.blurb: How heat, pressure and fluids change rock, how to read metamorphic grade, and where metamorphism happens.

units.title: Folds and Faults
units.blurb: How rocks bend and break under stress, and how geologists describe tilted and folded layers.

units.title: Geologic Time
units.blurb: Ordering events with Steno's principles and unconformities, dating rocks with radioactive clocks, and the great events of Earth's history.

units.title: Plate Tectonics in Depth
units.blurb: Measuring plate motion, what drives it, the anatomy of each kind of boundary, and how oceans open and close.

units.title: Earthquakes
units.blurb: Why faults slip, locating an earthquake, measuring its size and shaking, forecasting the odds, and tsunamis.

units.title: Landscapes
units.blurb: Slopes, rivers, floods, groundwater and glaciers: the processes that shape the land and the numbers that describe them.

units.title: Earth Resources
units.blurb: How ore deposits and fossil fuels form, and how reserves are counted.

topics.title: How Earth Formed and Layered
topics.short: Earth grew from colliding rock and metal about 4.54 billion years ago and, while hot, sorted itself by density into core, mantle and crust.
topics.trouble: Students think Earth's age comes from its oldest rocks; those are about 4 billion years old because early crust was recycled, so the 4.54-billion-year age comes from meteorites and Moon rocks.

topics.title: Seeing Inside Earth with Seismic Waves
topics.short: S waves can't cross the liquid outer core and P waves bend at its edge, leaving shadow zones that map the core.
topics.trouble: Students think scientists found Earth's layers by drilling; the deepest hole reached only about 12 km, and the layers were found from how seismic waves travel.

topics.title: Heat Flow and the Geothermal Gradient
topics.short: Temperature rises about 25 °C per kilometer in the upper crust, fed by heat left from Earth's formation and by radioactive decay.
topics.trouble: Students carry the crust's rate all the way down, which would make the center about 160,000 °C; the gradient is steep only near the surface, and the center is about 5,000 to 6,000 °C.

topics.title: Isostasy: How Crust Floats
topics.short: Crust floats on the mantle like ice on water, so high mountains have deep roots and land rises when an ice sheet melts.
topics.trouble: Students think mountains sit on a flat base held up by solid rock; like an iceberg, a high range is balanced by a thick root of crust reaching down into the denser mantle.

topics.title: Earth's Magnetic Field in Rocks
topics.short: Earth's field flips now and then, and iron-rich minerals in cooling lava record its direction, building a timeline of reversals.
topics.trouble: Students picture a giant bar magnet of iron in the core; the core is far too hot to stay magnetized, and the field is made by liquid iron moving in the outer core.

topics.title: Atoms, Ions and Crystals
topics.short: A mineral is ions stacked in a repeating pattern, and ions of similar size and charge can trade places, so a mineral's makeup can vary.
topics.trouble: Students think a mineral's formula is always exact; olivine ranges from Mg₂SiO₄ to Fe₂SiO₄ because iron and magnesium ions have about the same size and charge.

topics.title: The Silica Tetrahedron
topics.short: One silicon bonded to four oxygens, SiO₄ with a charge of −4, is the building block of most minerals in the crust.
topics.trouble: Students get the tetrahedron's charge wrong; one Si⁴⁺ and four O²⁻ give +4 − 8 = −4, and sharing oxygens between tetrahedra lowers the charge.

topics.title: Silicate Families
topics.short: Tetrahedra link as singles, chains, double chains, sheets or 3-D frameworks, which sets each mineral's silicon-to-oxygen ratio and how it breaks.
topics.trouble: Students memorize silicate names without their structures, so it seems arbitrary that mica peels into sheets and quartz has no cleavage at all; both follow from how the tetrahedra link.

topics.title: Carbonates, Oxides, Sulfides and Other Groups
topics.short: Sort minerals by their negative ion: carbonates (CO₃), oxides (O), sulfides (S), sulfates (SO₄), halides (Cl, F) and native elements.
topics.trouble: Students mix up sulfides and sulfates; pyrite (FeS₂) is a sulfide with no oxygen, while gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) is a sulfate.

topics.title: How Rocks Melt
topics.short: Rock in the mantle melts when the pressure drops, when water is added, or when hot magma heats the crust around it.
topics.trouble: Students think magma forms only by heating; under mid-ocean ridges and hot spots rock melts because it rises and the pressure drops, and at subduction zones water lowers its melting point.

topics.title: Bowen's Reaction Series
topics.short: As magma cools, minerals crystallize in order: olivine and calcium-rich feldspar first, quartz last.
topics.trouble: Students think a magma crystallizes all its minerals at once; they form over a range of temperatures, and the leftover melt grows richer in silica.

topics.title: Mafic to Felsic
topics.short: Magmas range from mafic (low in silica, hot, runny and dark) to felsic (high in silica, cooler, sticky and light).
topics.trouble: Students think the hottest lava is the most explosive; hot basalt is runny and erupts gently, while cooler, silica-rich magma traps gas and explodes.

topics.title: Naming Igneous Rocks
topics.short: Name an igneous rock from its texture and composition: granite and rhyolite, diorite and andesite, gabbro and basalt.
topics.trouble: Students name a rock by its color alone; texture tells where it cooled, so granite and rhyolite share a composition but differ in crystal size.

topics.title: Plutons, Dikes and Sills
topics.short: Magma that cools underground forms batholiths, dikes that cut across layers and sills that slip between them.
topics.trouble: Students mistake a sill for a buried lava flow; a sill bakes the rock above and below it, while a buried lava flow bakes only the rock beneath.

topics.title: Gentle and Explosive Eruptions
topics.short: Viscosity and gas decide whether magma oozes out as lava or blasts out as ash; the VEI rates eruptions by volume, ten times more per step.
topics.trouble: Students think the volcano with the biggest lava flows is the most dangerous; Kīlauea pours out large flows gently, while the sticky magma of Mount St. Helens blasted out explosively.

topics.title: Volcanic Hazards and Monitoring
topics.short: Pyroclastic flows, lahars, ash, gases and lava each threaten in their own way; swelling ground, gas and small earthquakes can give warning.
topics.trouble: Students think a quiet volcano is dead; many rest for centuries between eruptions, and monitoring watches for swelling, gas and earthquakes to spot one waking.

topics.title: Chemical Weathering Reactions
topics.short: Feldspar turns to clay, iron minerals rust and calcite dissolves, while quartz resists and piles up as sand.
topics.trouble: Students think the minerals that crystallize first are the toughest; it is the reverse: olivine weathers fastest at the surface, and quartz, which crystallizes last, lasts longest.

topics.title: Grain Size and the Wentworth Scale
topics.short: Sort sediment by size, from clay under 1/256 mm to boulders over 256 mm, and use the phi scale, φ = −log₂ d.
topics.trouble: Students expect phi to grow with grain size; the minus sign gives coarser grains smaller phi values, even negative ones.

topics.title: How Flowing Water Moves Sediment
topics.short: Faster water moves bigger grains; the Hjulström diagram shows when a grain is picked up, carried or dropped.
topics.trouble: Students think the smallest grains are always the easiest to pick up; sticky clay takes faster water to erode than sand does, though once lifted it stays afloat in very slow water.

topics.title: Sorting, Rounding and Maturity
topics.short: The farther sediment travels, the better sorted and rounder it gets and the more of it is quartz.
topics.trouble: Students think "well sorted" means sorted into separate layers; it means the grains in one sample are about the same size.

topics.title: Naming Sedimentary Rocks
topics.short: Name clastic rocks by grain size and shape (conglomerate, breccia, sandstone, shale) and chemical and biochemical rocks by makeup (limestone, rock salt, chert, coal).
topics.trouble: Students think limestone is sand cemented together; most limestone is calcite from shells and other skeletons.

topics.title: Reading Sedimentary Structures
topics.short: Cross-beds, ripple marks, mud cracks and graded beds show current direction, waves, drying out and which way was up.
topics.trouble: Students read every ripple the same way; ripples with even, symmetric crests come from waves sloshing back and forth, while lopsided ones show which way a current flowed.

topics.title: Depositional Environments
topics.short: Match rocks and structures to the place they formed: river, delta, beach, reef, deep sea, desert dunes or glacier.
topics.trouble: Students think a rock formed where it is found today; marine limestone and fossil shells high in the Himalayas formed on an ancient seafloor that was later pushed up.

topics.title: Heat and Pressure with Depth
topics.short: Pressure grows by about 26 MPa for each kilometer of rock overhead (P = ρgh), and temperature rises along the geotherm.
topics.trouble: Students think pressure alone lines up minerals into layers; pressure that is equal on all sides only squeezes, and foliation needs stronger squeezing in one direction.

topics.title: Foliation and Metamorphic Grade
topics.short: As heat and pressure rise, shale becomes slate, phyllite, schist and then gneiss, and index minerals like garnet appear in order.
topics.trouble: Students treat slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss as unrelated rocks; they can be one parent rock cooked to higher and higher grade.

topics.title: Naming Metamorphic Rocks
topics.short: Name a metamorphic rock by its foliation and its parent: marble from limestone, quartzite from sandstone, gneiss from granite or shale.
topics.trouble: Students confuse quartzite with sandstone; quartzite breaks right through its grains, while sandstone breaks around them.

topics.title: Where Metamorphism Happens
topics.short: Contact metamorphism bakes rock beside magma, regional metamorphism comes with mountain building, and subduction makes high-pressure, low-temperature rocks.
topics.trouble: Students think all metamorphism needs deep burial; a hot intrusion can bake the rock beside it close to the surface.

topics.title: Stress and Strain
topics.short: Rocks are squeezed, stretched or sheared; near the surface they break (brittle), while deep and hot they bend (ductile).
topics.trouble: Students think solid rock can't bend; given heat, pressure and time, rock folds like warm wax without breaking.

topics.title: Anticlines, Synclines and Domes
topics.short: Folds arch up (anticlines) or sag down (synclines); once eroded, an anticline shows its oldest rocks in the middle.
topics.trouble: Students assume an anticline is a hill and a syncline is a valley; erosion often wears the land flat, so folds are found by the pattern of rock ages, not by the shape of the land.

topics.title: Normal, Reverse and Strike-Slip Faults
topics.short: Name the hanging wall and footwall and read the slip: pulling apart makes normal faults, squeezing makes reverse and thrust faults, and shearing makes strike-slip faults.
topics.trouble: Students decide a fault's type by which side stands higher today; the type depends on how the hanging wall moved compared with the footwall.

topics.title: Strike and Dip
topics.short: Strike is the compass direction of a level line on a tilted layer, dip is its downward tilt, and with trigonometry they give how deep the layer lies.
topics.trouble: Students draw the dip direction along the strike; dip always points straight down the slope of the layer, at a right angle to the strike.

topics.title: Steno's Principles and Faunal Succession
topics.short: Original horizontality, lateral continuity, inclusions and the order of fossils extend superposition to read any outcrop.
topics.trouble: Students think tilted layers were laid down tilted; sediment settles in flat layers, so the tilting came later.

topics.title: Unconformities
topics.short: A buried erosion surface marks missing time: an angular unconformity, a nonconformity or a disconformity.
topics.trouble: Students think an unconformity is a kind of layer; it is a gap in the record, a surface where rock was worn away or never laid down.

topics.title: Correlating Rock Layers
topics.short: Match layers from place to place by rock type, by key beds such as volcanic ash, and by index fossils.
topics.trouble: Students match layers by thickness or color alone; the same kind of rock can form at different times, so fossils and key beds are stronger clues.

topics.title: Reconstructing a Region's History
topics.short: Put a cross-section's events in order: deposition, folding, faulting, intrusion, erosion and more deposition.
topics.trouble: Students list events in the order of the layers from bottom to top and forget the tilting, faulting and erosion that happened between them.

topics.title: Radiometric Dating
topics.short: From the ratio of daughter to parent atoms, find how many half-lives have passed: a ratio of 1 means one half-life, 3 means two, 7 means three.
topics.trouble: Students think carbon-14 dates dinosaur bones and ancient rocks; with a half-life of 5,730 years it works only for once-living material up to about 50,000 years old.

topics.title: Choosing a Radioactive Clock
topics.short: Match the clock to the job: carbon-14 for recent remains, potassium–argon and uranium–lead for igneous rock millions to billions of years old.
topics.trouble: Students try to date a sandstone directly; its grains are older than the rock, so sedimentary layers are dated by the igneous rocks above, below or cutting them.

topics.title: Combining Relative and Absolute Ages
topics.short: Date a sedimentary layer by the dated igneous rocks around it: younger than what lies below it, older than what cuts it or covers it.
topics.trouble: Students give a single age when the evidence only brackets a range; a shale between ash beds dated 95 and 92 million years old is somewhere between those ages.

topics.title: Major Events in Earth's History
topics.short: Place the big events on the time scale: the oldest minerals, first life, oxygen in the air, the Cambrian explosion and the great mass extinctions.
topics.trouble: Students think the air always had oxygen; for its first two billion years Earth's air had almost none, until photosynthesizing microbes built it up about 2.4 billion years ago.

topics.title: Magnetic Stripes and Spreading Rates
topics.short: Match seafloor stripes to the reversal timeline to find how fast a ridge spreads, as a half rate or a full rate.
topics.trouble: Students mix up half and full spreading rates; each plate moves away from the ridge at the half rate, and the two plates separate at twice that.

topics.title: Measuring Plate Motion with GPS
topics.short: GPS stations move millimeters to centimeters a year; subtracting their velocity vectors shows how two plates move relative to each other.
topics.trouble: Students read each station's arrow as motion relative to its neighbor; to see whether a boundary opens or closes, subtract one station's velocity from the other's.

topics.title: What Drives the Plates
topics.short: Sinking slabs pull plates, high ridges push them, and the mantle convects beneath; the pull of sinking slabs is the largest force.
topics.trouble: Students picture plates as rafts carried along by mantle currents; the fastest plates are the ones with long sinking edges, which shows the sinking slab itself pulls hardest.

topics.title: Subduction Zones
topics.short: The denser plate sinks, earthquakes trace the slab hundreds of kilometers down, and water from the slab melts the mantle above to feed arc volcanoes.
topics.trouble: Students think the sinking plate melts to make the arc's magma; the slab mostly stays solid, and the water it gives off lowers the melting point of the mantle above it.

topics.title: Continental Collisions and Rifts
topics.short: Continents are too buoyant to sink far, so they crumple into high mountains when they meet and stretch into rift valleys when they split.
topics.trouble: Students expect continents to subduct like ocean floor; continental crust is too light to sink far, so collisions thicken it into ranges like the Himalayas.

topics.title: Transform Faults
topics.short: Transform faults offset mid-ocean ridges and let plates slide past each other, and only the part between the ridge segments is active.
topics.trouble: Students read the offset of a ridge as the direction of slip; between ridge segments the plates often slide the opposite way to what the offset suggests.

topics.title: The Wilson Cycle
topics.short: Oceans open and close in a cycle (rift, young ocean, wide ocean, subduction, closing and collision), with supercontinents like Pangaea in between.
topics.trouble: Students think Pangaea was Earth's first and only supercontinent; there were others before it, such as Rodinia about a billion years ago.

topics.title: Elastic Rebound
topics.short: Rock on both sides of a locked fault bends slowly, then snaps back in an earthquake; slip rate and slip per quake give the average time between quakes.
topics.trouble: Students think many small earthquakes release the strain and prevent a big one; it takes about 1,000 magnitude 5 quakes to release the energy of one magnitude 7.

topics.title: Distance from the S–P Time
topics.short: P waves outrun S waves, so the gap between their arrivals grows with distance: d = Δt·vP·vS/(vP − vS).
topics.trouble: Students try to find the distance from the P-wave arrival alone; without knowing when the quake began, one arrival can't give the distance, but the gap between P and S can.

topics.title: Finding the Epicenter
topics.short: Draw a circle of the right distance around each of three stations; the epicenter is where all three circles meet.
topics.trouble: Students think two stations are enough; two circles usually cross at two points, and a third station picks the right one.

topics.title: Moment Magnitude and Energy
topics.short: Magnitude grows with the logarithm of the fault's area times its slip, and each step up means about 32 times more energy.
topics.trouble: Students think magnitude 10 is the top of a 1-to-10 scale; the scale has no top, but no known fault is long enough to make a magnitude 10.

topics.title: Intensity and Ground Shaking
topics.short: Intensity measures the shaking at one place on the Modified Mercalli scale; it depends on distance, depth and soft ground, not only on magnitude.
topics.trouble: Students think an earthquake has a single intensity; each quake has one magnitude but many intensities, strongest near the epicenter and on soft, wet ground.

topics.title: Earthquake Forecasts as Probabilities
topics.short: Turn a yearly chance into the chance of at least one event in n years: 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ.
topics.trouble: Students add yearly chances, so 2% a year for 30 years seems like 60%; the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.98³⁰, about 45%.

topics.title: Tsunamis
topics.short: A sudden jolt of the seafloor lifts the whole water column; the wave crosses deep ocean as fast as a jet (v = √(gd)) and slows and grows tall near shore.
topics.trouble: Students picture a tsunami as one giant breaking wave like surf; it is a series of very long waves, the first is often not the largest, and each can flood inland for many minutes.

topics.title: Landslides and Slope Stability
topics.short: A slope fails when the downhill pull beats the friction and strength holding it; water and steeper slopes tip the balance.
topics.trouble: Students think water makes a slope fail mainly by its weight; water filling the pores pushes the grains apart and lowers their friction.

topics.title: Stream Gradient and Discharge
topics.short: A stream's gradient is its drop per distance, and its discharge is width × depth × speed, in cubic meters per second.
topics.trouble: Students think a steep mountain stream is faster and carries more water than a big river downstream; the gentler river often flows faster on average and carries far more water.

topics.title: Meanders, Floodplains and Base Level
topics.short: Rivers wear away the outside of bends and build on the inside, spread floodplains, and cut down toward base level.
topics.trouble: Students think the fastest water is on the inside of a bend because that path is shorter; it is on the outside, which is why the outer bank wears away.

topics.title: What a 100-Year Flood Means
topics.short: Rank a river's yearly peak flows to find recurrence intervals; a 100-year flood has a 1% chance of happening in any year.
topics.trouble: Students think a 100-year flood comes once a century, so after one the next is 100 years away; the chance is 1% every year, and two can come in back-to-back years.

topics.title: Groundwater Flow and Darcy's Law
topics.short: Groundwater flows from high head to low head, and Darcy's law, Q = K·A·Δh/L, tells how much.
topics.trouble: Students think groundwater flows as fast as a stream; it creeps through pores, often less than a meter a day, so a pollutant can take years to reach a well.

topics.title: Glaciers: Mass Balance and Flow
topics.short: A glacier gains snow up high and loses ice down low; its end advances or retreats with the balance, but the ice always flows downhill.
topics.trouble: Students think a retreating glacier flows backward uphill; the ice keeps flowing forward, but its end melts faster than new ice arrives.

topics.title: How Ore Deposits Form
topics.short: Ores are rare places where geology concentrated a metal; magma, hot water, weathering, evaporation and rivers can all do it.
topics.trouble: Students think a metal can be mined wherever it occurs; copper averages about 60 parts per million in the crust, and ore needs it concentrated about 100 times or more.

topics.title: How Oil, Gas and Coal Form
topics.short: Buried remains of tiny sea life cook into oil at about 60 to 120 °C and collect under a seal in a trap, while buried swamp plants become coal.
topics.trouble: Students think oil comes from dinosaurs; most oil formed from tiny algae and plankton buried in seafloor mud.

topics.title: Resources, Reserves and How Long They Last
topics.short: Reserves are the part of a resource that can be produced at a profit today, so the years they last change with price, technology and discovery.
topics.trouble: Students read "reserves ÷ yearly use = 40 years" as the date a resource runs out; reserves grow and shrink with prices, technology and new discoveries.
